title: POLYamine treatment in elderly patients with Coronary Artery Disease (POLYCAD): study protocol for a Danish randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of spermidine treatment versus placebo

sections.abstract:
Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Caloric restriction promotes cardiovascular health but is difficult to sustain. Spermidine, a naturally occurring polyamine and caloric-restriction mimetic, has been linked to improved longevity in epidemiological studies and shown to enhance autophagy, mitochondrial function, and cardiovascular ageing in preclinical models. This trial will investigate whether high-dose spermidine improves cardiac remodelling, exercise capacity, muscle mass, and systemic inflammation in elderly patients with CAD.

This is a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, superiority trial at Aarhus University Hospital, Denmark. We have randomised 187 patients aged ≥ 65 years with CAD (prior coronary artery revascularisation or myocardial infarction ≥ 3 months prior to screening) and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (> 40%) in a 1:1 ratio to receive either 24 mg/day spermidine or placebo for 48 weeks. Participants, investigators, outcome assessors, and data analysts will remain blinded until completion of the analysis of all primary endpoints. Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. The trial is powered to detect between-group differences in four co-primary endpoints: (1) left ventricular mass (g) by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, (2) peak oxygen consumption (mL·kg⁻ 1 ·min⁻ 1 ) by cardiopulmonary exercise testing, (3) appendicular lean mass (g) by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and (4) high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (mg/L). Secondary outcomes include 24-h ambulatory blood pressure, arterial stiffness, physical performance, muscle strength, daily physical activity, quality of life, cognitive function, dietary spermidine intake, and spermidine levels in plasma and skeletal muscle. Safety monitoring includes laboratory testing, telephone interviews and adverse event recording.

This is the first trial to investigate the cardiovascular and metabolic benefit from a high-dose spermidine treatment in patients with CAD. The findings will provide important insights into the therapeutic potential of spermidine.

ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT06186102 (first posted 12 June 2023). Participant enrolment began on 4 January 2024, and trial completion is anticipated in August 2026.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s13063-025-09176-z.
sections.introduction:
Life expectancy has increased significantly over the past century. As the global elderly population continues to expand, ageing-related health challenges become increasingly relevant. Promoting healthy ageing is therefore essential to enhancing longevity, improving quality of life and addressing socioeconomic challenges. Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, accounting for one-third of all deaths. Coronary artery disease (CAD) contributes to approximately 16% of global deaths [ 1 ] and 12% of all deaths in Denmark [ 2 ].

Fasting and caloric restriction can extend life and improve health in a plethora of organisms, including rodents and non-human primates [ 3 ]. Pharmacological treatments that replicate the beneficial effects of caloric restriction are of particular interest. In this context, the naturally occurring polyamine spermidine has garnered attention [ 3 , 4 ]. Polyamines are found in all forms of life and are essential for cell growth and proliferation. Spermidine is found in all plant-derived foods, particularly in wheat germ, soybeans, mushrooms, peas, nuts, vegetables and fruits [ 5 ]. It is absorbed in the small intestine, enters the circulation, and is rapidly utilised for essential cellular processes throughout the body [ 6 , 7 ].

In humans, high spermidine intake is inversely associated with mortality and morbidity [ 8 – 12 ], with all-cause mortality decreasing by approximately 63% (40.5 to 15.1 deaths per 1000 person-years) across increasing intake in a 20-year longitudinal study [ 8 ]. Interestingly, blood levels decline with age, raising the possibility that supplementation strategies could enhance health span [ 9 , 13 – 15 ]. Supporting these findings, spermidine has been shown to prolong lifespan in various organisms, including yeast, worms, flies, and mice, while also inducing autophagy, enhancing mitochondrial function, and attenuating cardiovascular ageing [ 9 , 16 , 17 ]. This raises the question of whether elderly patients with cardiovascular disease could benefit from treatment with this polyamine. ClinicalTrials.gov currently lists two other ongoing clinical studies on spermidine intervention, both investigating conditions other than those in the present study (Supplementary Table 1). Previous trials have examined spermidine treatment at lower doses and shorter durations, while others have explored spermidine-rich diets, such as natto, or combined spermidine with compounds such as nicotinamide.

Polyamine treatment in elderly patients with coronary artery disease (POLYCAD) is the first Phase II trial to comprehensively assess high-dose spermidine treatment over 48 weeks in a large CAD population, providing an extended treatment duration and an evaluation of its potential cardiovascular and metabolic benefits.

The primary objective of POLYCAD is to determine whether daily treatment with 24 mg of spermidine for 48 weeks improves four co-primary endpoints, assessed at baseline and after intervention (see Outcomes).

Secondary objectives are to evaluate effects on additional cardiovascular, metabolic, and functional outcomes.

Safety objectives are to monitor and report potential adverse effects related to high-dose spermidine supplementation, although none are anticipated (see “Adverse event reporting and harms {22}”).

POLYCAD is a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, superiority trial testing the cardiovascular and metabolic benefits of 24 mg/day spermidine versus placebo in elderly patients with CAD. A total of 187 patients have been enrolled and randomised 1:1 to receive either three 8 mg spermidine capsules (total 24 mg) or three matching placebo capsules daily for 48 weeks. Participants will undergo assessments at baseline within 14 days before randomisation and after the 48-week intervention, with a follow-up window of 4 weeks. sections.methods:
This investigator-initiated trial is conducted at Aarhus University Hospital with approval from the Danish National Ethical Committee. The trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06186102 ). The investigators are solely responsible for the study design, conduct, data collection, management, statistical analysis, interpretation, and reporting. The funding bodies have no role in any of these processes and no authority over the content or the decision to submit the final manuscript. The protocol adheres to the SPIRIT guidelines, with the completed checklist provided.

Patients with CAD are recruited by the investigators from the outpatient clinic at the Department of Cardiology, Aarhus University Hospital, Denmark (see CONSORT diagram, Fig. 2 ). sections.discussion:
Each primary endpoint reflects a distinct mechanistic domain: cardiac remodelling, physical performance, body composition, inflammation, aligning with preclinical evidence of spermidine’s pleiotropic effects.

Epidemiological evidence supports the beneficial effects of polyamines, including spermidine, on health outcomes [ 9 , 10 ]. Higher dietary spermidine intake has been associated with reduced mortality and morbidity. Notably, Kielch et al. reported an inverse relationship between spermidine intake, assessed through food questionnaires, and both all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in the 20-year Bruneck cohort study, which included 829 participants. [ 8 ]. In the same cohort, dietary spermidine intake was inversely associated with the risk of both fatal and clinically overt heart failure, with high intake linked to an approximately 40% lower risk compared to low intake groups [ 9 ]. Additionally, spermidine intake correlated with lower blood pressure and a reduced risk of composite cardiovascular events, including acute myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular death [ 9 ].

Epidemiologic studies have demonstrated a significant correlation between daily spermidine intake and various obesity-associated metabolic parameters, including BMI, waist circumference, and markers of insulin resistance. Specifically, higher spermidine intake is linked to lower fasting serum glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c levels, and a reduced HOMA-IR [ 28 ].

Together, these studies emphasise the therapeutic potential of spermidine in promoting cardiometabolic health.

In geriatric mouse models, spermidine induces autophagy in skeletal muscle stem cells (MuSC), reversing cellular senescence and enhancing muscle repair and regeneration [ 29 ]. This hypothesis is supported by a recent study on spermidine’s effects on eIF5A, promoting activation of MuSCs [ 30 ]. In another study, spermidine ameliorated myopathic defects and mitochondrial dysfunction in collagen-VI–deficient mice [ 31 ]. Furthermore, spermidine, both independently and in combination with exercise, effectively alleviated skeletal muscle atrophy in an ageing rodent model induced by D-galactose [ 32 ]. Further, studies have demonstrated spermidine-induced ultrastructural and functional improvements in mitochondria from aged cardiac muscle and MuSCs [ 9 , 31 , 32 ].

Given its promising effects, further research on spermidine’s role in preserving or improving skeletal muscle mass and function in elderly individuals is warranted. To our knowledge, no previous study has investigated spermidine’s effects on skeletal muscle in humans.

An interventional study testing a dietary fasting mimetic formulation containing spermidine (15 mg), nicotinamide, palmitoylethanolamide, and oleoylethanolamide, found acute beneficial effects on anti-inflammatory markers in humans [ 33 ]. Another investigation demonstrated that a 2-month two times daily dietary supplementation with a combination of spermidine (0.6 mg), AM3 (a patented glycophosphopeptical complex) and hesperidin (a plant-based polyphenolic compound), reduced markers of biological age and enhanced immune functions versus placebo [ 34 ]. The inclusion of multiple substances in a single supplement, however, complicates the ability to attribute specific effects to spermidine alone.

Spermidines anti-inflammatory properties has been investigated particularly in LPS-stimulated murine microglial cells, where it reduced pro-inflammatory mediators such as tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and Interleukin-6 (IL-6) [ 35 ]. Spermidine lowered TNF-α levels in mice compared to placebo and reduced macrophage infiltration and inflammatory responses in both the liver and white adipose tissue [ 9 , 28 ].

These findings support the hypothesis that spermidine plays a role in regulating inflammation and highlight its potential as a therapeutic strategy for age-related inflammation.

Spermidine supplements marketed for the improvement of cognition are commercially available; however, spermidine’s effects on cognition are not well established. Dietary spermidine intake, assessed via food frequency questionnaires, correlated with improved cognitive function and reduced cognitive decline in humans, based on data from the Bruneck Study [ 36 ]. Higher spermidine intake was associated with better Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores and a lower risk of cognitive impairment (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.51–0.78, p < 0.001). The relationship followed a dose–response pattern and remained significant after adjusting for confounders, including dietary patterns. Findings align with experimental models supporting a potential role of spermidine in cognitive health [ 36 ].

The daily dose of 24 mg of spermidine in POLYCAD was chosen based on considerations of dietary spermidine content, findings from toxicology animal studies, and previous clinical studies, with the objective to balance safety with efficacy. The study dose of 24 mg will be 3–10 times higher than in most commercially available spermidine supplements. This dose is considered high, but not a supraphysiological spermidine treatment since average daily nutritional intake of spermidine can vary from 7 to 25 mg [ 18 ]. In a recent study, a spermidine treatment of 40 mg per day for 28 days was safe and well-tolerated in healthy older men, with no significant changes in serum polyamine content and only minimal increases in urinary spermidine and spermine in comparison with placebo [ 27 ]. Interestingly, spermidine treatment appeared to prevent the postprandial decline in plasma spermidine in another investigation, indicating a role in maintaining homeostasis rather than directly elevating circulating levels [ 33 ]. This aligns with prior research demonstrating increased spermidine concentrations during fasting, which suggests a dynamic regulation of polyamine levels depending on metabolic states [ 37 ]. In a placebo-controlled trial with a spermidine wheat germ extract, which provided 1.2 mg spermidine, 0.6 mg spermine, and 0.2 mg putrescine per day, no differences in blood polyamine concentrations were observed between the control group and spermidine-supplemented older adults after 3 months of dietary supplementation [ 38 ]. Similarly, in a 12-month trial with a 0.9 mg spermidine dose, polyamine concentrations remained unchanged [ 39 ]. In another clinical trial, healthy adults consumed natto, a polyamine-rich food providing 5.4–10.3 mg per day, for 26 weeks [ 40 ]. In a subsequent trial, a form of natto richer in spermidine was consumed for 12 months. The estimated spermidine and spermine intakes were 7–21 mg and 2.5–6.5 mg per day, respectively, in the intervention group [ 41 ]. Both trials showed increased spermine concentrations in healthy adults without changes in spermidine levels. A selective increase in plasma spermine following dietary spermidine and spermine intervention underlines the complexity of polyamine metabolism, in which enzymatic activity, transporter functions, and tissue uptake, all are likely to be crucial regulators. No interventional study of spermidine in humans has measured increased plasma spermidine concentrations, suggesting extensive first-pass metabolism, absorption and conversion before systemic circulation. Previous studies have shown that orally ingested spermidine undergoes rapid absorption in the small intestine and is metabolised in enterocytes or the liver, leading to elevated plasma spermine rather than spermidine. For instance, oral spermidine intervention (15 mg/day) elevated plasma spermine but not spermidine, supporting the hypothesis of conversion during hepatic first-pass metabolism [ 42 ]. This metabolic behaviour is corroborated by findings in rat models, where over 60% of spermidine was absorbed within 10 min, primarily undergoing conversion or tissue uptake, especially in the skeletal muscle tissue [ 43 ]. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has examined polyamine content in human tissues following spermidine supplementation. In POLYCAD, we will measure spermidine, spermine, and putrescine levels in both plasma and the skeletal muscle tissue, before and after 48 weeks of intervention.

Toxicity of dietary polyamines has not been reported in humans [ 19 ]. In a rat toxicity study, the no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) for spermidine was 83 mg/kg body weight/day, with weight loss observed at higher doses [ 44 ]. In contrast, the polyamine, spermine had a significantly lower NOAEL (19 mg/kg body weight/day), and extremely high doses (> 200 mg/kg body weight/day) led to aggressive behaviour, paralysis, and even death. These severe adverse effects were not observed in rats receiving spermidine [ 44 ]. Applying a 100-fold safety factor (10 for interspecies differences × 10 for intraspecies variability), a daily spermidine dose below 40 mg is considered safe for humans weighing 50 kg or more, while a 24 mg dose is expected to pose no risk of adverse effects. A more recent toxicological study in rats, published after conceptualization of the POLYCAD study protocol, suggests that even higher doses may be safe. Although rats receiving the highest doses experienced weight loss, no other physical or biochemical signs of toxicity were observed [ 45 ].

The POLYCAD trial aims to test the benefits of spermidine on cardiovascular health, skeletal muscle mass and function, whole-body composition, inflammation, and cognition in patients with CAD. This exploratory approach allows for the simultaneous investigation of multiple outcomes each testing a specific hypothesis, aligning with findings from preclinical animal studies and epidemiological research on polyamine intake and health.

The Bonferroni or hierarchical correction is commonly used to control the risk of Type I error when multiple comparisons are performed. In this study, however, the four co-primary endpoints assess distinct organ systems, each representing separate hypothesis and clinically relevant outcomes. Applying a Bonferroni or hierarchical correction in this context may be overly conservative, increasing the risk of Type II errors and potentially obscuring meaningful effects. Given the limited commercial interest in spermidine as a therapeutic option, these research questions may otherwise remain unexplored. Therefore, multiple endpoints were included within a single study framework. Any statistically significant findings will require further validation in larger randomised trials, focusing on a single primary endpoint.

Given the 48-week study duration, we selected appropriate endpoints to assess cardiovascular and metabolic health. The POLYCAD trial is not powered to detect differences in mortality or major cardiovascular events between groups. While 48 weeks may be insufficient to observe long-term clinical outcomes such as effects on longevity that have been seen in animal models, this study establishes a new benchmark for the duration of spermidine intervention trials.

The first study protocol: “Polyamine treatment in elderly patients with coronary artery disease—a randomised controlled trial” was approved by the Central Denmark Region Committees on Health Research Ethics on June 26, 2023. The Protocol version 5.0 was approved with amendments on 4 April 2024. Recruitment began on 4 January 2024 and was completed in August 2025, after submission to Trials . The final study visit is expected in August 2026.
